title: The GR57 Ourthe Valley Walking Week

bestPeriod.note: Summer school holidays (July–August) bring the kayak and campsite crowds to the river villages; late spring and September keep the valley quiet.

summary: A week of GR57 river-valley walking along the Ourthe from La Roche-en-Ardenne, through gorges, dams and the Ardennes' oldest bourgs.
hook: This is not alpine walking and it does not pretend to be. The Ourthe cuts a deep, wooded valley through the Ardennes plateau, and the GR57 follows it — up one bank, down the other, through beech forest, past castle ruins and into small stone towns that have been market centres since the Middle Ages. A week here is quiet, well-marked and genuinely hilly, without a single lift or hut.

snapshot.Base(s): La Roche-en-Ardenne, with day loops and two out-nights toward Hotton and Durbuy
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 95–115 km, 2,600–3,200 m cumulative ascent; forested valley slopes, riverside path, farm track, waymarked red-and-white GR
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Brussels (BRU), train to Marloie or Melreux-Hotton, then TEC bus to La Roche-en-Ardenne
snapshot.Who It Suits: Steady walkers who want real daily distance and hills without alpine exposure; a good first multi-day hiking trip

itinerary.title: La Roche-en-Ardenne orientation loop
itinerary.morning: Arrive and climb straight to the Château de La Roche-en-Ardenne, a ruined feudal fortress on its rock spur above the Ourthe, to get the shape of the valley before walking it for real.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop out to Le Deister, the wooded viewpoint above town, and back down through the old streets near the market square.
itinerary.evening: A first Ardennes dinner — jambon d'Ardenne and a local Orval or Rochefort — at one of the riverside restaurants along the Quai de l'Ourthe.
itinerary.dayStats: 9 km, 250 m ascent, 250 m descent. Waymarking: local yellow-rectangle circuit around town, not yet the GR57.

itinerary.title: La Roche to Nisramont
itinerary.morning: Join the GR57 heading upstream along the Ourthe Occidentale, following the riverbank through mixed forest with the water never far below the path.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb to the Nisramont dam and its reservoir, a working hydroelectric barrage that also created a quiet lake popular with local anglers; loop back on the opposite bank.
itinerary.evening: Return to La Roche by the same waymarked route or by a short taxi transfer if legs are tired — this is a there-and-back day, deliberately, to keep the same base.
itinerary.dayStats: 20 km, 550 m ascent, 550 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 red-and-white horizontal bars throughout, well maintained.

itinerary.title: Ourthe Occidentale toward Ortho
itinerary.morning: Continue upstream past Maboge, where the valley narrows and the path climbs onto the wooded slope above the river before dropping back to water level.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Ortho, a small hamlet with a working watermill history, then return via a higher forest track that gives long views back down the valley toward La Roche.
itinerary.evening: A rest evening — this stretch is the longest out-and-back of the week and legs earn an early night.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 600 m ascent, 600 m descent. Waymarking: GR57, with a short shared stretch on a local yellow-marked variant near Ortho.

itinerary.title: La Roche to Marcourt and the château ruins loop
itinerary.morning: Shorter day, deliberately. Walk downstream and cross to Marcourt, where the ruins of another Ardennes château sit above the confluence of the Ourthe's two branches.
itinerary.afternoon: A forest loop above Beausaint gives a genuinely quiet stretch of the valley, with beech and oak canopy and almost no other walkers outside peak summer weekends.
itinerary.evening: Back in La Roche by mid-afternoon; use the extra time to visit the small Musée de la Bataille des Ardennes, a reminder of how contested this valley was in December 1944.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 400 m ascent, 400 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 to Marcourt, local blue-marked circuit for the Beausaint loop.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Hotton, walk to Barvaux
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi transfer downstream to Hotton, known locally for its show caves (Grottes de Hotton) carved into the valley's limestone band — a genuine geological break from the schist and sandstone upstream.
itinerary.afternoon: Pick up the GR57 heading downstream along the Ourthe toward Barvaux-sur-Ourthe, a flatter, more open stretch of valley than the upper river, with willow and alder lining the banks.
itinerary.evening: Overnight in Barvaux, a small riverside town with a long tradition of Ourthe kayak tourism, quiet outside July and August.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 300 m ascent, 300 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 red-and-white, flat and well-signed.

itinerary.title: Barvaux to Durbuy and back
itinerary.morning: Follow the riverside path from Barvaux to Durbuy, popularly (if imprecisely) marketed as the smallest town in the world — a genuinely well-preserved stone bourg with a topiary garden and a medieval street plan.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop back via the wooded ridge above the river rather than retracing the flat bank path, for a different angle on the valley before returning to Barvaux.
itinerary.evening: Transfer back to La Roche-en-Ardenne by bus in the early evening to close the loop on the same base for the final night.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 350 m ascent, 350 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 to Durbuy, local yellow-marked ridge path for the return.

itinerary.title: Nadrin and the Belvédère des Six Ourthes
itinerary.morning: A short bus or taxi ride to Nadrin, where the GR57 passes the Belvédère des Six Ourthes, a viewing tower over the river's tightest meanders — six loops of the Ourthe visible at once from the top.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the loop trail beneath the belvedere and back into La Roche-en-Ardenne along the final stretch of river valley, closing the week where it started.
itinerary.evening: A last dinner in La Roche, unhurried.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 300 m ascent, 300 m descent. Waymarking: GR57 throughout, the week's final and most scenic river-meander stretch.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gîte or chambre d'hôtes in La Roche-en-Ardenne
accommodationStrategy.description: La Roche has a long tradition of hosting Ardennes walkers and kayakers, and small guesthouses near the Quai de l'Ourthe are used to muddy boots and early breakfasts. Staying here for five of the seven nights keeps logistics simple.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–4 weeks ahead for summer weekends, less pressure outside July–August.

accommodationStrategy.name: Small hotel or gîte in Barvaux-sur-Ourthe
accommodationStrategy.description: The one night away from La Roche, chosen to make the Hotton–Barvaux–Durbuy stretch a two-day out rather than a long there-and-back; riverside guesthouses here are used to walkers arriving on foot with packs.

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering cottage near La Roche
accommodationStrategy.description: A number of Ardennes gîtes rent by the week with a kitchen, useful for keeping food costs down across seven days.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European, the standard number across Belgium for police, fire and ambulance.
logistics.money: Small-town shops and boulangeries often close on Mondays and for a long lunch; stock up on picnic supplies the afternoon before a long walking day.
logistics.transportRules: TEC regional buses link La Roche-en-Ardenne, Hotton, Barvaux and Nadrin, but frequency drops sharply outside weekday commuting hours — check the return timetable before setting out each transfer day.

other.label: Waymarking system
other.text: Belgium uses the same GR convention as France: a horizontal red bar over a horizontal white bar means continue straight; the same two bars crossed into an X means wrong way; an angled double bar means turn. Local circuit walks (PR, Promenades) use single-colour rectangles — yellow, blue or green — maintained by local tourism offices rather than the GR federation, and often overlap the GR57 for short stretches.

other.label: River levels
other.text: After heavy rain the lowest riverside stretches near Hotton and Barvaux can flood the path; a higher parallel forest track exists at most points and is signed as an alternative.

other.label: Hunting season
other.text: Parts of the Ardennes forest are open to organised hunts (chasse) from autumn through winter, signed at access points; this trip's May–June/September window largely avoids it, but check local signage in September.

other.label: Wild camping is not permitted
other.text: on the marked GR network in Wallonia; overnight stops are gîtes, chambres d'hôtes or hotels in the valley towns.

proTips: Walk the Nisramont and Ortho out-and-backs (Days 2–3) in the morning light heading upstream — the river runs roughly east–west here and the low sun sits behind you on the return leg.

Buy Ardennes ham and a wedge of Orval-washed cheese at a Hotton or Barvaux boulangerie for a riverside picnic rather than eating in a restaurant every midday — it is cheaper and lets you time the walk around the food, not the other way round.
Visit the Grottes de Hotton first thing on Day 5, before the transfer walk — the caves get warm foot traffic from midday coach groups in season.
Climb the Belvédère des Six Ourthes on a clear morning rather than late afternoon; low-angle morning light shows the river meanders far better than a flat midday sun.
Ask your La Roche gîte host about the Musée de la Bataille des Ardennes' opening hours before Day 4 — it is a small, volunteer-run museum with limited hours outside peak season.
Time the Durbuy loop for a weekday. The town is genuinely small and a summer Saturday brings coach parties that overwhelm its narrow streets.
Carry a paper IGN or NGI 1:25,000 map alongside the waymarking — GPS signal is reliable in the valley but the marking itself is the more dependable navigation tool here, as it should be.

packingNotes: Sturdy trail shoes rather than heavy boots — the terrain is wooded valley slope, not alpine rock, and drains well.
A light rain shell; Ardennes weather turns from sun to drizzle with little warning even in a good week.
A 20–25 L daypack is enough; nights are spent in guesthouses, not huts, so no sleeping gear is needed.
A refillable water bottle — village fountains and café taps cover most days, but carry 1–1.5 L for the longer out-and-back stages.
Insect repellent for the river-adjacent forest stretches in early summer.
A paper NGI/IGN Ardennes walking map as backup to the GR waymarking.
Cash in small denominations — several village boulangeries and small gîtes are cash-preferred.
What people over-pack: technical hiking gear. This is a serious walking week, but it is hills and forest, not mountains — trail shoes and a rain shell cover nearly everything.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Heavy rain floods the lowest riverside path.** Fallback: take the signed higher forest alternative that parallels most of the GR57's low sections near Hotton and Barvaux.
**A TEC bus transfer is missed or delayed.** Fallback: La Roche and the river towns are close enough (12–20 km) that a taxi transfer is a realistic, inexpensive backup.
**A gîte in Barvaux has no room on short notice.** Fallback: book that one mid-week night well ahead, since it is the trip's only fixed away-night and the town's guesthouse stock is small.
**Tired legs after the long Day 3 out-and-back.** Fallback: Day 4 is deliberately shorter and closer to base — treat it as the built-in recovery day it is.
**Hunting activity signed near a forest section in early autumn.** Fallback: respect the posted diversion and use the parallel valley-floor GR57 route, which hunts rarely close.
